messages.subject: updates...
messages.body_plain:
The fifth sprint of work to update the GBM package has finished.  The aim of the sprint was to update the Cox proportional hazards distribution with code provided by Terry Therneau.  This has mostly been achieved with room left for further enhancements in the future.  A short writeup of the changes to the CoxPH model has been written and is attached.

Because we're now at a state where we're fairly happy with the code, I've submitted a pull request against gbm-developers/gbm.  Please try it out, comment, suchlike.

https://github.com/gbm-developers/gbm/pull/79

The current sprint, sprint 6, is significantly shorter than those previously due to public holidays and other commitments.  As such, it will focus on developing a test plan for the package in preparation for subsequent testing and optimization sprints.  We'd really like to know of any tests that you'd like included with the package.

Hope this helps,

--
pdm

messages.subject: questions on Cox
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

We think we've got your Cox likelihood in there.  We've had to hack it a bit; adding in checks to account for the bagging done in gbm (essentially just adding in if statements to check if row X is in the bag.).  A couple of questions have arisen:

1. How should we get bagging, the train-test split, and cross-validation to be compatible with strata?  (A related question, if you've got panel data with multiple rows / subject, should we bag / cross-validate at the subject level rather than the row level?)

2. When we get down to assigning predictions to terminal nodes of each tree, can we get the "current" values of \eta into your cox regression code using offset?  [otherwise we have to write something that's almost, but not exactly, the same as your coxph?]  If we can't do that, can you give us any help on how we can do this part of the gbm algorithm?  For the moment we've left the old Cox fit-best-constant code in there, but it shouldn't be too hard to change.

Thanks,

--
Paul

messages.subject: Re: questions on Cox
messages.body_plain:
To deal with strata isn't the obvious approach to stratify the
cross-validation (or the selection of the training set) to ensure all
CV folds contain at least some observations from each stratum? There's
functionality to do that for binomial response to ensure all CV
samples have some successes and some failures. If a particular stratum
has so few observations that the number of CV folds is too high, the
user should be told that.

If a subsample within a CV fold doesn't see a particular stratum, does
that matter so long as it doesn't produce an error? Each tree in the
collection is supposed to be weak, so does it make a big difference if
some of them are ignorant of certain strata?

Regarding subsampling / CV for panel data, I'd propose to subsample
patients. Otherwise, don't you create a missing data problem that is
unlikely to be representative of the observed data? To introduce
randomness within sampled patients would require a parametric model, I
think, unless the time-ordering is irrelevant (which it won't ever
be). So far as I understand, the effect of subsampling is to stop the
algorithm finding a local minimum too quickly, so I don't think we
need to worry too much if the randomness created by subsampling
somewhat over, or under, represents true sampling variation (which is
something to worry about if formal inference is being based on a
bootstrap scheme, but that's a different setting).

messages.subject: Re: questions on Cox
messages.body_plain:
On 05/03/2016 04:03 AM, Paul Metcalfe wrote:
> Hi!
>
> We think we've got your Cox likelihood in there.  We've had to hack it a bit; adding in checks to account for the bagging done in gbm (essentially just adding in if statements to check if row X is in the bag.).  A couple of questions have arisen:
>
> 1. How should we get bagging, the train-test split, and cross-validation to be compatible with strata?  (A related question, if you've got panel data with multiple rows / subject, should we bag / cross-validate at the subject level rather than the row level?)

Good questions.  First the easy one: if there are multiple rows per subject, then cross-validation, bagging, train-test, etc should always work with entire subjects.  In the survival package the control code for this is has a split personality: some routines use cluster(id) within the formula, some use id= as another argument, and some allow both.  I have been divided as to which form is "most natural" for a user.

 The id argument is easier to code: add "id" to the line at the top of the code.
   m <- match(c("formula", "data", "weights", "offset", "id"), names(mf), 0)
Then add
    id <- model.extract(mf, "id")
a little further down, e.g., where you fetch the weights.  If you use cluster() then steal code from my coxph routine.  You have to fetch the id and then remove it from the model so it doesn't end up in the X matrix.

Strata.  Conceptually, in a Cox model strata are treated as separate data sets and the statistic of interest is computed as a sum over the strata.  That's what the loglik is in the code I sent: loglik within strata, summed. Martingale residuals are computed within strata and then the vectors are concatonated rather than added.  The first derivative of the loglikelihood for a stratified model is technically (first deriv for strata 1) = u1 X1 + (first derviative for strata 2) = u2 X2 + .....  where u1 = martigale residuals for everyone in the first stratum, X1 = X matrix rows for the first stratum, u2 = residuals for strata 2 etc.  But with matrix multiplication this is the same as  (u1, u2, u3,...) X, so we don't have to worry about it.
   To apply this to Cox-gbm: I hadn't really thought about what the current routine does.  My first reaction is that the natural candidate is the cross-validated partial likelihood of van Houwelingen, but that is a fair bit of work.  I need to re-read the paper and see what was done in order to give a detailed response on the details.  I'll try to do that this week.  Four other projects are clamoring, but a fifth really needs the gbm code.

>
> 2. When we get down to assigning predictions to terminal nodes of each tree, can we get the "current" values of \eta into your cox regression code using offset?  [otherwise we have to write something that's almost, but not exactly, the same as your coxph?]  If we can't do that, can you give us any help on how we can do this part of the gbm algorithm?  For the moment we've left the old Cox fit-best-constant code in there, but it shouldn't be too hard to change.
>

I'm a little confused.  The code I sent has a single parameter "eta" for the risk score, which is the predicted X beta for each subject.  That prediction might be from a separate data set, or not.  Are you using a call to coxph in the test/validation suite?  If so, then yes the offset argument will do just what you want.

> Thanks,
>
> --
> Paul

messages.body_plain:
Thanks!

I agree on the CV / subsampling / whatnot. Just wanted to ensure that we all thought the same thing!

Re fitting: your coxph ends up with everyone in the same node having the same linear predictor. But because we're looking for the correction term, we need everyone to have the same correction to their previous linear predictor. Hence we have to get the "old" linear predictor in via offset. I think?

pdm

messages.subject: Can someone help to review the change to fix the pairwise and Bernoulli distribution?
messages.subject_clean: Can someone help to review the change to fix the pairwise and Bernoulli distribution?
messages.body_plain:
https://github.com/gbm-developers/gbm/pull/80

Recently introduced issues cause this two distributions don't function properly.
For the pairwise, ComputerLambda() is not working - adZ[] updating has been commented out unless NOISY_DEBUG is defined. This means the pairwise distribution is not functioning unless the GBM is complied with the NOISY_DEBUG flag.
For the Bernoulli: in InitF() its Newton method termination condition is incomplete: most likely it will terminate after one iteration. And since the commit[1], adOffset[] is not NULL in all cases; so the Newton process always is applied. The model will need more trees to fit the problem because of the unoptimized initialization.

They still exist after the major refactor change in #79 <https://github.com/gbm-developers/gbm/pull/79>

On 6 May 2016 02:13, "psheng@a9" <entel...@gmail.com> wrote:

> we have a half-baked internal version of parallelization based on multi-threads, prepare to submit back.
>
> 0. the parallelization is done for tree growth: according to my profiling, this phase contributes 90%+ of current training times;
> 1. it parallelizes by having one threads per features in the best split selection phase. for other dimensions to divide:
>      a. nodes: the gbm only evaluates two nodes in each split iteration(others are calculated and cached), so parallelization by nodes might not have big gain;
>      b. training samples: continuous features are processed in a sorted way, not easily to be parallelized; there might be some space for categorical features;
> 2. the performance improvement is related to the features number, and we observe the parallelization shortens the training time somehow;
> 3. the parallelization won't change the training result, the model will be exactly same;
> 4. IMO, single machine multi-thread is good enough: for millions of training sample with 0.5 bagging: one split takes around 1s on a upgraded server with multiple cores after parallelization. because aggregating/updating through entire training data is required after each boosting and reassignment of training data is needed after each split, distributed computing on multiple machines will be bounded by communication and might not help too much.
>
> for the next step:
> 1. would this change worth to be submit back?
> 2. there is a major refactor going on now, and seems the tree growth code has been changed a lot according to the pull request 79. should we wait the refactoring complete and migrate this change to the new version, or submit a pull request for what we have?
>
>
